sources.title: T. Brady and C. Watt, Lattices in finite real reflection groups, arXiv:math/0501502; Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 360 (2008), 4809-4844
sources.locator: Sections 2-7, arXiv PDF pp. 2-25 (pp. 4809-4832 of the published version): the reflection-length partial order and moved-space calculus (section 2), the Petrie root enumeration and the mu-dot-rho identities (section 3), the complex X(gamma) and its subcomplexes (sections 4-5), the walls of fat simplices (section 6) and the characterisation of |X(sigma)| and the lattice theorem (section 7). Section 8 (generalised associahedra) was read only at the level of its opening statements; sections 1 and the appendix were read only for orientation.

contents.name: Section 2: the reflection-length partial order l(w) = l(u) + l(u^{-1}w), the moved space M(A) = im(A - I), the fixed space F(A) = ker(A - I), and the uniqueness theorem for orthogonal B with M(B) = V and B <= A
Section 2: the reflection set S_alpha = {R in R : R <= alpha} determines alpha <= gamma, and delta with delta <= alpha, beta and S_delta = S_alpha cap S_beta is the greatest lower bound
Section 2, items (1)-(7): the moved-space monotonicity and rigidity (4) 'if alpha, beta <= delta and M(alpha) contained in M(beta) then alpha <= beta'
Section 3: the Steinberg bipartite labelling, the recursion rho_i = R_1...R_{i-1} alpha_i, the dual vectors mu_i, Theorem 3.2 gamma mu_i = mu_i - 2 rho_i and Corollary 3.3
Section 3, Theorem 3.7 (a)-(d): the sign and vanishing identities for mu_i . rho_j, and Corollary 3.8 on the separation of rho_k from the positive cone on earlier roots

Section 3, Lemma 3.9: for a consistently ordered subset the identity l(R(sigma_1)...R(sigma_k) gamma) = n - k is equivalent to mu(sigma_i) . sigma_j = 0 for i > j; the proof uses that l(R(sigma_k)...R(sigma_1)) = k by linear independence
Section 4, Definition 4.1 and Note 4.2: the abstract simplicial complex X(gamma) with vertex set the positive roots and simplices the subsets with R(rho_{i_k})...R(rho_{i_1}) <= gamma
Section 5: Theorem 5.1 and Note 5.2 (the canonical simple system delta_1,...,delta_k of P and its recursive determination), Theorem 5.4 (the rank-two description of X(sigma)) and Lemmas 5.5, 5.6
Section 6: Proposition 6.2 (sigma = R(epsilon_k)...R(epsilon_1)), Theorem 6.11 and Corollary 6.12 (the lexicographically first top simplex theta_1 < ... < theta_k of X(sigma))
Section 6, Examples 6.13 (B_4, sigma = [1,2,3]) and 6.14 (A_3, where the epsilon-ordering is inconsistent with the global order)
contents.reason: The two worked examples illustrate the reordering of the epsilon-roots in the source's own coordinates; the companion page instead computes the full interval and the Kreweras complements in S_4 through cycle supports, which is the type-A computation the design requests.

contents.name: Section 7, Propositions 7.1, 7.2: the action of sigma^{-1} on P and the separating-root lemma with the two constructed roots tau_b, tau_c
Section 7, Definition 7.3, Theorem 7.4, Corollary 7.5: X(sigma) is a simplicial complex of dimension l(sigma) - 1
Section 7, Theorem 7.6: c[X(sigma, tau_i)] = Y(sigma, tau_i) = Z(sigma, tau_i), the cone identification with the prescribed halfspaces
Section 7, Corollary 7.7: |X(sigma)| is convex, equals S^{n-1} cap c[P], and equals S^{n-1} cap M(sigma) cap mu(theta_1)^+ cap ... cap mu(theta_k)^+

Section 7, Theorem 7.8: the interval [I, gamma] is a lattice; the proof intersects X(alpha), X(beta), uses that |X(alpha) cap X(beta)| is a union of d-dimensional simplices spanning a common linear subspace, and sets sigma = R(v_d)...R(v_0)
Section 7, the purity sentence used in the proof of Theorem 7.8 ('for each d-simplex ... the linear subspaces span(v_0,...,v_d) and span(X) coincide')
Section 8: the embedding of X(gamma) into EX(gamma) and the sphere realisation related to generalised associahedra
contents.reason: The generalised associahedron sphere and its type-W generalisations are a separate geometric development not needed for the lattice, conjugacy and Kreweras results of this pair; the design explicitly declines the associahedron route for this page.

contents.name: Section 1: the second Garside structure of finite-type Artin groups and the motivation from the Birman-Ko-Lee monoid
contents.reason: The Garside and classifying-space applications belong to the Artin-group and Hopf-Hecke parts of the track; this pair only needs the lattice and complement structure of the absolute interval, which is developed without them.

sources.title: D. Armstrong, Generalized Noncrossing Partitions and Combinatorics of Coxeter Groups, Mem. Amer. Math. Soc. 202 (2009), no. 949, arXiv:math/0611106v2
sources.locator: Chapter 2, sections 2.4-2.6 (printed pp. 22-34) and Chapter 4, sections 4.1-4.2 (printed pp. 82-89). The remaining chapters (in particular the invariant-theoretic Catalan computation of section 2.7, the nonnesting and cluster developments of Chapter 3 and the refined type-B and type-D models of Chapter 4) were not read for this batch.

contents.name: Definition 2.4.4: the absolute order pi <=_T mu iff l_T(mu) = l_T(pi) + l_T(pi^{-1} mu), and Theorem 2.4.7 identifying l_T(w) with dim Mov(w)
Shifting Lemma 2.5.1 and Subword Property 2.5.2: reduced T-words and the subword characterisation of the absolute order
Definition 2.5.3 and Lemma 2.5.4: the map K^nu_mu(pi) = mu pi^{-1} nu is an anti-automorphism of the interval [mu, nu] with l_T(K^nu_mu(pi)) = l_T(mu) + l_T(nu) - l_T(pi)
The complement remark preceding section 2.6: on a lattice interval the Kreweras complement is a lattice complement, pi vee K(pi) = nu and pi wedge K(pi) = mu

Definition 2.6.1 and Lemma 2.6.2: standard Coxeter elements are products of the simple generators in an order; any two standard Coxeter elements are conjugate, the moved space of a Coxeter element is V, and every reflection lies below every Coxeter element
Definition 2.6.7: NC(W, c) = [1, c] as the interval in Abs(W), with the remark that conjugacy of Coxeter elements makes its isomorphism type independent of c
Theorem 2.6.6 (Bessis): the parabolic Coxeter elements are exactly the elements lying below some Coxeter element
contents.reason: Parabolic Coxeter elements and the parabolic-subinterval-isomorphism argument belong to the induction theory of NC(W) but are not needed here: the meet and join construction of this pair works directly with the ordered root complex, so the parabolic route is not consumed.

contents.name: Theorem 2.6.12: NC(W) is a lattice (Bessis case by case, uniform proof of Brady-Watt)
Proposition 2.6.9 and the Kreweras complement notation 2.6.10: pi -> Mov(pi) is a poset embedding of NC(W) and K = K^c_1 is the Kreweras complement
Lemma 2.6.13: a reduced T-word satisfies w = t_1 vee ... vee t_r, and pi mu in NC(W) with pi <=_T pi mu or mu <=_T pi mu implies pi mu = pi vee mu
contents.reason: The join lemma is used by Armstrong to compare the group and lattice structures inside NC(W); the lattice operations of this pair are constructed through the meet of common upper bounds, so the join lemma is not required and is not reproved.

contents.name: Section 2.7: invariant theory and the classical Catalan and Fuss-Catalan enumeration of NC(W)
contents.reason: The design explicitly declines an unproved Catalan-cardinality product for general types; the abstract invariant-degree machinery of section 2.7 belongs to the invariant-theory page of this track and is not consumed by the two theorems here.

contents.name: Definition 4.1.1, Theorem 4.1.2: NC(n) as the refinement lattice of noncrossing partitions of [n], with blockwise-intersection meets and the Catalan and Narayana counts of Kreweras
Lemma 4.1.4: right multiplication by a transposition (i j) splits a cycle when i, j are in the same cycle and joins two cycles otherwise, and Lemma 4.1.5: l_T(pi) = n - number of cycles
Theorem 4.1.3 (Biane): the cycle-support map pi -> {pi} is an isomorphism NC(A_{n-1}) -> NC(n), with the splitting argument for surjectivity and the orientation argument for injectivity

Definition 4.2.2 and Definition 4.2.3: the interleaving of two partitions on the 2n-gon and the classical Kreweras complement as the coarsest interleaving partner; the rotation and self-bijection properties and the block count n - m + 1
Identity (4.4): w_P . w_{K(P)} = c, relating the classical Kreweras complement to the group-theoretic complement
Theorem 4.1.2(3) and section 4.4: the zeta polynomial, Fuss-Catalan numbers and multichain enumeration of NC(n)
contents.reason: Multichain and Fuss-Catalan enumerations of the noncrossing lattice are not among the promised claims of this pair, whose type-A content is the cycle-support model and the Kreweras complement rather than the generating-function enumeration.

sources.title: H. Eriksson and K. Eriksson, Conjugacy of Coxeter elements, Electron. J. Combin. 16(2) (2009), #R4
sources.locator: The complete 7-page article: Introduction (rotation equivalence, Theorem 1.1) and section 2 (edge orientations, chip firing, Proposition 2.1, Corollary 2.2 and Proposition 2.3 on trees and cycles).

contents.name: Introduction and Theorem 1.1: Coxeter elements are conjugate if and only if their words are rotation equivalent; the statement that the tree and cycle cases were known earlier
Section 2: the translation between Coxeter words and acyclic edge orientations of the Coxeter graph, with rotation as conjugation by the first letter
Proposition 2.3, tree case: a tree with n nodes has 2^{n-1} acyclic orientations but only one reachability class under sink/source firings, by induction on a leaf
Proposition 2.3, cycle case: an n-cycle has n-1 reachability classes of firing moves, so Coxeter elements of affine type can fall into several conjugacy classes
contents.reason: The affine and cyclic multiplicity of conjugacy classes is the sharpness companion of the tree theorem but is not needed for finite type, where every finite-type diagram is a tree and the single-class conclusion suffices.
